title.source: Section check: Civics, Media & Everyday Economics
title.back: Section check: Civics, media and everyday economics

intro.source: 10 questions about Lessons 20–24. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.
intro.back: 10 questions about Lessons 20–24. No need to hurry. You can go back to the lessons and try again as many times as you like.

questions.0.question.source: Which of these is a need, not a want?
questions.0.question.back: Which is a need, not a want?
questions.0.question.note: "need" / "want" as สิ่งที่จำเป็น / สิ่งที่อยากได้ (KEY_TERMS).

questions.0.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Music videos are nice, but you can live without them. That makes them a want. Look back at Lesson 20.
questions.0.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. Music videos are nice, but you can live without them, so they are a want. Go back to Lesson 20.

questions.0.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. A new football is fun, but you can live without it. That makes it a want. Look back at Lesson 20.
questions.0.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. A new football is fun, but you can live without it, so it is a want. Go back to Lesson 20.

questions.0.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. You must have clean water to live and stay healthy. That makes it a need.
questions.0.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. You must have clean water to live and stay healthy, so it is a need.

questions.1.stimulus.body.source: Amani and two friends share one tablet at a made-up learning centre. They have 30 minutes left on it today. They can play a word game or watch a short science video. There is not enough time for both. They choose the science video.
questions.1.stimulus.body.back: Amani and two friends share one tablet at a fictional learning centre. Today they have 30 minutes of use left. They can play a word game or watch a short science video, but there isn't enough time for both. They choose to watch the science video.

questions.1.question.source: What is the opportunity cost of their choice?
questions.1.question.back: What is the opportunity cost of this choice?

questions.1.options.0.text.source: The word game they do not play
questions.1.options.0.text.back: The word game they didn't play

questions.1.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. The word game is the next-best thing they give up. That is their opportunity cost.
questions.1.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. The word game is the next-best thing they gave up. That is their opportunity cost.
questions.1.options.0.feedback.note: "the next-best thing they give up" as สิ่งที่ดีรองลงมาที่พวกเขายอมสละ. Check it is clear to a 12-year-old. Second pass: "give up" now ยอมเสียไป, the words Lesson 20 uses for opportunity cost (was ยอมสละ). Second pass: Now uses Lesson 20's own words (สิ่งที่ดีรองลงมาที่...ยอมเสียไป), which the lesson already explains. Flag removed.

questions.1.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The video is what they choose. The opportunity cost is what they give up. Look back at Lesson 20.
questions.1.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. The video is what they chose. The opportunity cost is what they gave up. Go back to Lesson 20.
questions.1.options.1.feedback.note: Second pass: "give up" now ยอมเสียไป, the words Lesson 20 uses for opportunity cost (was ยอมสละ).

questions.1.options.2.text.source: The tablet that they all share

questions.1.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The tablet is a resource they use. The opportunity cost is the thing they give up. Look back at Lesson 20.
questions.1.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. The tablet is the resource they use. The opportunity cost is what they gave up. Go back to Lesson 20.
questions.1.options.2.feedback.note: Second pass: "give up" now ยอมเสียไป, the words Lesson 20 uses for opportunity cost (was ยอมสละ).

questions.2.question.source: Here is a made-up example. Jun fixes a broken chair for Lucia. In return, Lucia teaches Jun a card game. No money is used. What is this kind of exchange called?
questions.2.question.back: This is a fictional example. Jun fixes Lucia's broken chair. In return, Lucia teaches Jun a card game. No money is used. What is this kind of exchange called?
questions.2.question.note: Second pass: "In return" now เป็นการตอบแทน, as in Lesson 21; เพื่อตอบแทน could be read as Jun fixing the chair "to repay" Lucia.

questions.2.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Scarcity means there is not enough for every use. Here, two people swap skills with no money. Look back at Lesson 21.
questions.2.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. Scarcity is not having enough for every use. Here, two people swap skills without money. Go back to Lesson 21.
questions.2.options.0.feedback.note: Second pass: ทุกการใช้, Lesson 20's wording for "every use".

questions.2.options.1.text.note: "barter" as การแลกของกับของ (KEY_TERMS). The Thai term is longer than the two wrong options (ความขาดแคลน, งบประมาณ), so the checker warns that the right answer is clearly the longest; in English "Barter" is not. Left as is to keep the KEY_TERMS word; a reviewer should decide whether it stands out too much. Second pass: Kept: Lesson 21 uses the same term (การแลกของกับของ), and its picture now does too.

questions.2.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. Barter means swapping a thing or a skill without using money. Jun and Lucia swap skills.
questions.2.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. Barter is swapping things or skills without using money. Jun and Lucia swap skills.

questions.2.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. A budget is a plan for money or time. Here, two people swap skills with no money. Look back at Lesson 21.
questions.2.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. A budget is a plan for using money or time. Here, two people swap skills without money. Go back to Lesson 21.

questions.3.question.source: Lesson 21 says every exchange depends on trust. What happens when a seller cheats?
questions.3.question.back: Lesson 21 says every exchange depends on trust. What happens when a seller cheats?

questions.3.options.0.text.source: More people want to buy from them.
questions.3.options.0.text.back: People want to buy from the seller more

questions.3.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. People do not want to buy from someone who cheats. Look back at Lesson 21.
questions.3.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. People don't want to buy from someone who cheats. Go back to Lesson 21.

questions.3.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. If someone cheats, people stop trusting them. Then trade gets harder for everyone.
questions.3.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. If someone cheats, people stop trusting them, and then trade gets harder for everyone.
questions.3.options.1.feedback.note: Second pass: การค้าขาย, as Lesson 21 says in the same sentence.

questions.3.options.2.text.source: Nothing changes at the market at all.

questions.3.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Cheating breaks trust, and then trade gets harder for everyone. Look back at Lesson 21.
questions.3.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. Cheating destroys trust, and then trade gets harder for everyone. Go back to Lesson 21.
questions.3.options.2.feedback.note: Second pass: การค้าขาย, as Lesson 21 says in the same sentence.

questions.4.question.source: Mei's time budget has 15 minutes for reading English and 15 minutes for games on the shared phone. What does this show?
questions.4.question.back: Mei's time budget has 15 minutes for reading English and 15 minutes for playing games on the shared phone. What does this show?

questions.4.options.0.text.source: A budget can plan time, not only money.
questions.4.options.0.text.back: A budget can plan time, not just money

questions.4.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. Budgets are not only for money. Mei uses a budget to plan her time in the evening.
questions.4.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. A budget isn't only for money. Mei uses a budget to plan her evening time.

questions.4.options.1.text.source: A budget means Mei can never play games.
questions.4.options.1.text.back: The budget means Mei can't play games at all

questions.4.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Mei still has 15 minutes for games. She just has less time for them. Look back at Lesson 22.
questions.4.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. Mei still has 15 minutes to play games, just less time. Go back to Lesson 22.

questions.4.options.2.text.source: A budget is only ever a plan for money.
questions.4.options.2.text.back: A budget is a plan for using money only

questions.4.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Mei's budget is a plan for her time. Budgets are not only for money. Look back at Lesson 22.
questions.4.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. Mei's budget is a plan for using time. A budget isn't only for money. Go back to Lesson 22.

questions.5.question.source: Lesson 22 says that small, short goals are useful. Why?
questions.5.question.back: Lesson 22 says small, short-term goals are useful. Why?

questions.5.options.0.text.source: They do not need any steps or plan.
questions.5.options.0.text.back: They need no steps or plans at all

questions.5.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. You still work towards a goal step by step. Look back at Lesson 22.
questions.5.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. You still have to go step by step to reach a goal. Go back to Lesson 22.

questions.5.options.1.text.source: They make sure nothing will ever change.
questions.5.options.1.text.back: They make sure nothing changes at all

questions.5.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Plans can still change. That is why a small goal you can work on now helps. Look back at Lesson 22.
questions.5.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. Plans can still change. That is why small goals you can start now help. Go back to Lesson 22.

questions.5.options.2.text.source: You can start to work on them now.
questions.5.options.2.text.back: You can start them right now

questions.5.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Plans can change, but you can work on a small goal now. One example is learning 10 new words a week.
questions.5.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. Plans may change, but you can start small goals now, for example learning 10 new words a week.

questions.6.stimulus.title.source: Message F, a made-up message from Lesson 23
questions.6.stimulus.title.back: Message F, a fictional message from Lesson 23
questions.6.stimulus.title.note: "Message F" as ข้อความ F: keep the letter as Lesson 23 labels its messages.

questions.6.stimulus.items.0.source: A photo of a fish as long as a bus.
questions.6.stimulus.items.0.back: A photo of a fish as long as a bus

questions.6.stimulus.items.1.source: The words say: “Caught at Lakeside yesterday.”
questions.6.stimulus.items.1.back: The message says "Caught at Lakeside yesterday"

questions.6.stimulus.items.2.source: The edges of the fish look strange.
questions.6.stimulus.items.2.back: The edges of the fish look strange

questions.6.stimulus.items.3.source: Nobody else has a photo of this fish.
questions.6.stimulus.items.3.back: No one else has a picture of this fish

questions.6.question.source: Which detail is a clue that the photo may not be real?
questions.6.question.back: Which detail is a clue that this photo may not be real?

questions.6.options.0.text.source: It is a photo, not a written message.
questions.6.options.0.text.back: It is a photo, not written text

questions.6.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. A photo can be real or changed. Being a photo does not show it is fake. Look back at Lesson 23.
questions.6.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. A photo may be real or edited. Being a photo doesn't show it is fake. Go back to Lesson 23.
questions.6.options.0.feedback.note: Second pass: "changed (with an app)" now ถูกแต่ง, Lesson 23's word for an edited photo (was ถูกแก้ไข).

questions.6.options.1.text.source: The edges of the fish look strange.
questions.6.options.1.text.back: The edges of the fish look strange

questions.6.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. Strange edges can show that a photo was changed with an app. Also, nobody else has a photo of this fish.
questions.6.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. Strange-looking edges may show the photo was edited with an app, and also no one else has a picture of this fish.
questions.6.options.1.feedback.note: Second pass: "changed (with an app)" now ถูกแต่ง, Lesson 23's word for an edited photo (was ถูกแก้ไข).

questions.6.options.2.text.source: It says where the fish was caught.
questions.6.options.2.text.back: It says where the fish was caught

questions.6.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Naming a place does not show a photo is fake. Think about how the fish itself looks. Look back at Lesson 23.
questions.6.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. Naming a place doesn't show the photo is fake. Think about how the fish itself looks. Go back to Lesson 23.

questions.7.stimulus.body.source: Pia plays in a football team. She sees a message in a group chat. It says: “Our match at City Park is now on Sunday. Tell the whole team.” The message has no name and no date. Pia does not know who wrote it.
questions.7.stimulus.body.back: Pia plays on a football team. She sees a message in a group chat. It says "Our match at City Park has moved to Sunday. Tell everyone on the team." The message has no name and no date. Pia doesn't know who wrote it.
questions.7.stimulus.body.note: "City Park" (an invented place) kept in Latin letters like the other invented names; it could also be translated as สวนสาธารณะของเมือง. Check with Lesson 23. Second pass: Checked: Lesson 23 keeps City Park in Latin letters. Flag removed.

questions.7.question.source: What is the best thing for Pia to do first?

questions.7.options.0.text.source: Send it to the whole team right now
questions.7.options.0.text.back: Forward it to everyone on the team right away

questions.7.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The message has no name or date, so Pia cannot trust it yet. It is safer to check first. Look back at Lesson 23.
questions.7.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. The message has no name or date, so Pia can't trust it yet. Checking first is safer. Go back to Lesson 23.

questions.7.options.1.text.source: Believe it, because it sounds very sure
questions.7.options.1.text.back: Believe it, because it sounds very sure

questions.7.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. A message can sound sure and still be wrong. Pia needs to check it first. Look back at Lesson 23.
questions.7.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. A message may sound sure but not be true. Pia must check first. Go back to Lesson 23.
questions.7.options.1.feedback.note: "can sound sure and still be wrong" as ฟังดูมั่นใจ แต่ไม่จริงก็ได้ ("may not be true"), so the feedback never uses the word ผิด.

questions.7.options.2.text.source: Ask her coach if the message is true
questions.7.options.2.text.back: Ask the coach whether the message is true

questions.7.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Her coach is a trusted source. Pia can verify the message before she shares it.
questions.7.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. Her coach is a trustworthy source. Pia can check the message before forwarding it.
questions.7.options.2.feedback.note: Second pass: "trusted source" now แหล่งข้อมูลที่น่าเชื่อถือ, as Lesson 23 says.

questions.8.question.source: Lesson 24 says the bus users are stakeholders. What does that word mean?
questions.8.question.back: Lesson 24 says bus users are stakeholders. What does this word mean?
questions.8.question.note: "stakeholder" as ผู้มีส่วนเกี่ยวข้อง (KEY_TERMS, check). "bus users" as คนที่ใช้รถเมล์.

questions.8.options.0.text.source: A person or group that a problem affects
questions.8.options.0.text.back: A person or group affected by a problem
questions.8.options.0.text.note: Second pass: ได้รับผลจาก, the words of Lesson 24's definition of stakeholder.

questions.8.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. The litter at the bus stop affects the bus users and the centre manager. So they are stakeholders.
questions.8.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. The rubbish at the bus stop affects bus users and the centre manager, so they are stakeholders.

questions.8.options.1.text.source: A person who sells goods at a market stall
questions.8.options.1.text.back: People who sell goods at market stalls

questions.8.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The bus users are not selling anything. A stakeholder is someone a problem or plan affects. Look back at Lesson 24.
questions.8.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. Bus users don't sell anything. A stakeholder is a person affected by a problem or plan. Go back to Lesson 24.
questions.8.options.1.feedback.note: Second pass: ได้รับผลจาก, the words of Lesson 24's definition of stakeholder.

questions.8.options.2.text.source: A person who checks if a message is true
questions.8.options.2.text.back: People who check whether messages are true

questions.8.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Checking messages is part of Lesson 23. A stakeholder is someone a problem or plan affects. Look back at Lesson 24.
questions.8.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. Checking messages is the topic of Lesson 23. A stakeholder is a person affected by a problem or plan. Go back to Lesson 24.
questions.8.options.2.feedback.note: Second pass: ได้รับผลจาก, the words of Lesson 24's definition of stakeholder.

questions.9.question.source: What does Lesson 24 say about ways to help a community?
questions.9.question.back: What does Lesson 24 say about ways to help a community?

questions.9.options.0.text.source: Small, everyday actions can make a difference.
questions.9.options.0.text.note: "can make a difference" as ช่วยได้จริง (really helps); the literal สร้างความแตกต่าง sounds translated. The wrong option 1 uses the same words so the two stay parallel as in the English.

questions.9.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. Reading with a younger child or keeping a shared room clean can help a community.
questions.9.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. Reading with younger children, or helping keep a shared room clean, helps a community.

questions.9.options.1.text.source: Only big campaigns can make a real difference.

questions.9.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Helping does not have to mean a big campaign. Everyday actions matter too. Look back at Lesson 24.
questions.9.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. Helping doesn't have to be a big campaign; everyday actions matter too. Go back to Lesson 24.

questions.9.options.2.text.source: You must speak in public to help at all.
questions.9.options.2.text.back: You must speak in public to help

questions.9.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. You never need to speak in public, post online or take risks to help. Look back at Lesson 24.
questions.9.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. You don't need to speak in public, post online or put yourself in danger to help. Go back to Lesson 24.
questions.9.options.2.feedback.note: Lesson 24 (translate exactly). Kept all three things: speaking in public, posting online, taking risks.

results.high.back: Very well done. You know a lot about making choices, checking messages and helping a community.
